title: Arms Too Short for the Menu

patient.name: Mr Lim Boon Heng
patient.presenting_complaint: Difficulty reading small print up close for the past few months, especially the phone and restaurant menus

history.hpc: Mr Lim has noticed that small print is getting harder to read over the past few months. He says: 'Far away I can see clearly, but small letters on my handphone, I must stretch my arm until very far also still a bit blur.' It is worse in dim restaurant lighting and at the end of the day. Distance vision is fine. No pain, no double vision, no headaches.
history.pmhx: Nil significant. No previous eye conditions.
history.social_hx: Office worker, long hours on computer and phone. Reads physical documents daily. Non-smoker.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Normal bilaterally, clear lens both eyes
examination_findings.fundus: To be assessed by doctor as needed

investigations.va_distance: Modified LogMAR: RE 6/6, LE 6/6 unaided — distance vision is normal.
investigations.va_near: Near vision chart (N chart) held at 35 cm in good lighting, each eye tested separately: N10 unaided in each eye, improving to N5 when a +1.50 reading add is held up. Distance VA normal with reduced unaided near vision is the classic pattern of presbyopia.
investigations.iop_nct: RE 13 mmHg, LE 14 mmHg — normal range.

diagnosis: Presbyopia — age-related reduction in near focusing ability, shown by normal distance VA but reduced unaided near VA that improves with a near add. Typical onset around the late 40s. For doctor/optometrist to prescribe a reading correction.

immediate: Perform distance VA first (Modified LogMAR) to confirm distance vision is normal
Perform near VA using the N chart held at 35 cm in adequate lighting, testing each eye separately
Record the smallest line the patient can read comfortably (e.g., N10), and the improvement with a trial near add
Perform NCT for IOP as part of routine assessment
Maintain hand hygiene and alcohol-wipe the occluder and any near chart handling as per protocol
Document distance and near VA, the near add tested, and IOP for the doctor
follow_up: Doctor/optometrist to confirm the reading prescription (near add)
Discuss options: reading glasses, bifocals, or progressive lenses given his computer and phone use
Advise return if distance vision changes or other symptoms develop
patient_education: Explain that this is presbyopia — a normal age-related change in the eye's focusing, not a disease
Reassure him that distance vision is normal and only a reading correction is needed
Explain why he instinctively holds things further away (to bring the print into focus)
Suggest good lighting for near tasks and discuss suitable lens options with the doctor/optometrist

key_points: Establishes that the difficulty is specifically with near print while distance vision is fine
Identifies the habit of holding things further away and worse vision in dim light
Asks about age-relevant onset and visual demands (computer, phone, documents)
Rules out red flags (pain, double vision, headaches)
Confirms normal distance VA with Modified LogMAR first
Performs near VA with the N chart held at 35 cm in good lighting, each eye separately
Records the smallest comfortable near line and the improvement with a trial near add
Performs and documents NCT for IOP
Recognises the pattern of normal distance VA with reduced unaided near VA
Identifies this as presbyopia consistent with the patient's age
Understands that improvement with a near add confirms a focusing (not pathological) cause
Defers the final near prescription to the doctor/optometrist
Documents distance VA, near VA, near add tested, and IOP accurately
Explains presbyopia in simple, reassuring terms
Addresses the patient's lifestyle needs (computer/phone) when discussing options
Hands over to the doctor/optometrist for the reading correction
